script.opening: "So it’s diabetes, isn’t it. I could tell by how the receptionist said ‘the doctor wants a proper chat’. Look — I’ll be honest with you, doc, there’s not much point dressing it up. My dad had this. It took his eyes, then half his leg, then his heart at sixty-one. So whatever you’re going to tell me to do, I’ve kind of made my peace with where this goes. Just give me the tablets and I’ll get on with it."

facts.text: The engine of the consultation: dad diagnosed in his 40s, "never really did anything about it", went blind in one eye, below-knee amputation at 58, fatal MI at 61. Errol nursed him through the end. He has quietly decided diabetes is a death sentence on rails and that effort is futile.

HIDDEN AGENDA — under the breezy "give me the tablets" is despair: he believes the outcome is fixed, so why bother changing anything. This fatalism, not the HbA1c, is what will actually determine his next ten years. If unaddressed he will collect a prescription and change nothing.

If explored: he’s self-employed, drives for a living, no sick pay. A second, unspoken fear — does "diabetic" mean losing his licence, his income? He’s heard "they take your licence if you go on insulin." Hasn’t asked because he’s scared of the answer. If asked what he drives: a 3.5-tonne van on his ordinary car licence (Group 1), no lorry licence.
If asked non-judgementally: lives on garage food and energy drinks between drops, sits 11 hours a day, smokes 10/day, no time to exercise "with the job". Not lazy — trapped in a pattern by the work.

Officially: the tablets, then get on with it. Actually: to be told this is NOT automatically his father’s ending; that his dad’s era and untreated course are not his; that he can drive and earn; and a foothold of genuine agency rather than a leaflet.

ice.ideas: Diabetes is a one-way road to blindness, amputation and an early heart attack — his father’s exact path — and effort won’t change the destination.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fatalism/despair built on watching his father die of complications; plus an unspoken terror that the diagnosis will cost him his driving licence and his livelihood.
ice.expectations: Tablets and resignation. Underneath: to be shown that his father’s outcome is not preordained for him, that he can keep driving and earning, and a realistic first step he can actually take.

cues: "I’ve made my peace with where this goes" — fatalism, not acceptance; it is the real diagnosis to treat today.
"Give me the tablets and I’ll get on with it" — disengagement dressed as cooperation; a prescription alone changes nothing.
Any flicker at the word "insulin" or "licence" — the livelihood fear he hasn’t voiced.

checkpoints.text: Confirms and explains the diagnosis clearly (HbA1c diagnostic on two readings) without minimising or catastrophising; frames T2DM as serious but modifiable — a condition managed, not a sentence served

Directly addresses the father/fatalism: his dad’s untreated course in a different era is NOT Errol’s fixed fate; modern management (and the very fact he’s caught it now, asymptomatic) changes the trajectory — complications are largely preventable with control of glucose, BP, lipids and smoking

Negotiates an initial management plan collaboratively: lifestyle as genuine first-line (realistic for a driver — food swaps he can buy at a garage, walking at drops), metformin discussion, and — importantly — frames the option of remission given recent onset and weight (he meets the NHS Type 2 Diabetes Path to Remission criteria: aged 18–65, diagnosed within 6 years, BMI 27 or more), rather than "tablets for life"; drug treatment per NICE NG28: dual first-line therapy for most adults — modified-release metformin AND an SGLT2 inhibitor (unless contraindicated, or frailty makes the SGLT2 inhibitor risky), introduced stepwise: metformin first to check tolerability, then the SGLT2 inhibitor added once metformin is tolerated

Covers cardiovascular risk as the real killer: smoking cessation offered as the single highest-yield action (NICE NG209), BP confirmed with home or ambulatory readings (NICE NG136) and QRISK3 with a statin discussion (NICE NG238: atorvastatin 20 mg if QRISK3 is 10% or more), not just the glucose number

Answers the DVLA/livelihood question accurately and reassuringly, after first asking WHAT he drives (a delivery driver may hold a lorry licence): Group 1 (car and van up to 3.5 tonnes) on diet, metformin or an SGLT2 inhibitor needs no DVLA notification and no licence loss; Group 2 (lorry or bus) drivers must tell the DVLA if treated with tablets; insulin must be notified (Group 1 if longer than 3 months) and carries specific, manageable rules; he drives a van on a car licence, so he can keep driving — and gives him this proactively
Hears the despair under the cooperation and treats it as the priority, rather than handing over a prescription into a closed door
Explores the lifestyle without blame, recognising the job traps him in the pattern; builds the plan around his real day, not an idealised one

Arranges the diabetes-care scaffolding and follow-up: structured education referral at diagnosis (e.g. DESMOND; NICE NG28), NHS Diabetic Eye Screening referral, foot risk assessment (NICE NG19), bloods, the SGLT2 inhibitor sick-day rule once started, and a near review — leaving him with one concrete first step and a sense of agency, not a leaflet and a tablet

worked.txt: "You’ve told me the ending before we’ve started, and I understand why — you watched it happen to your dad. So let me be straight with you, because you’ve been straight with me: what happened to him is not what’s written for you. He was diagnosed in a different decade, and by his own account he never really treated it. You’re sitting here with no symptoms, caught early, with everything still working. That is a completely different starting line."

"Diabetes isn’t a countdown — it’s a number we can move. The eyes, the feet, the heart your dad lost: those come from years of high sugar, high pressure and smoking left unchecked. Control those and the complications largely don’t come. You’re not boarding your father’s train; you’re standing at a junction with a switch in your hand."

"Let me answer the thing I suspect you haven’t asked — first, what do you drive? … A van on your normal car licence. Then this does not cost you your licence. On diet or the tablets I’m suggesting, you don’t even tell the DVLA — you keep driving, you keep earning. If you ever drove a lorry on an HGV licence, the rules would be different, so tell me if that changes. If we ever needed insulin there are extra checks, but they’re manageable and plenty of drivers do them. Your livelihood is safe. Take that one off your shoulders right now."

"I’m not going to tell a man doing eleven-hour shifts to ‘eat more salmon and go to the gym’. Let’s be real: at the garage, the meal-deal water instead of the energy drink, the nuts instead of the pastry; a five-minute walk at every few drops. Small, repeatable, free. And the single biggest thing you could do for your heart isn’t a tablet — it’s the cigarettes. I’ll help you with that properly when you’re ready."

"And here’s something your dad was never offered: because you’ve caught this early and there’s weight we could shift, type 2 can sometimes go into remission — the number back to normal, off medication. There’s an NHS programme for exactly this, with total diet replacement, and you qualify. I’m not promising it, but it’s a goal worth aiming at, and it’s the opposite of ‘making your peace with where this goes’."

"So here’s the plan: the usual start now is two tablets that work as a pair — metformin today, and once it’s settled, in a few weeks, a second tablet that also protects the heart and kidneys; I’ll book you proper diabetes education, eye screening and a foot check — the things that catch problems before they’re problems. But the only homework today is one thing: swap the energy drinks for water this week. That’s it. Come back in two weeks and we build from there. You walked in expecting your father’s ending. You’re walking out with a switch in your hand."

f.learning: The new-T2DM consultation is not a data download — the HbA1c is the easy part. The examinable core here is the hidden agenda: fatalism built on a father lost to untreated complications, plus an unvoiced terror about the driving licence and livelihood. A prescription handed into that despair changes nothing. The skill is to treat the fatalism first — his father’s untreated course in another era is not Errol’s fixed fate; complications come from years of uncontrolled glucose/BP/lipids/smoking, all modifiable — and to answer the DVLA question proactively and accurately — having asked what he drives: on a car/van licence (Group 1), diet, metformin or an SGLT2 inhibitor means no notification and no licence loss; a Group 2 lorry licence would need notification on tablets. Then negotiate a plan built around his actual day, lead with smoking cessation as highest-yield CVD action, offer remission as a real goal given early onset (NHS Type 2 Diabetes Path to Remission Programme), start treatment per NICE NG28 (updated February 2026: metformin then an SGLT2 inhibitor), and leave him with one concrete step and genuine agency.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG28 (updated February 2026) · NICE NG19 · NICE NG238 · NICE NG136 · NICE NG209 · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (diabetes)
knowledge.summary: Two HbA1c results of 48 mmol/mol or more confirm type 2 diabetes. The first consultation sets engagement for years: treat the fatalism, answer the licence fear, then build a plan around his working day.

points.t: HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol or more on two occasions confirms diabetes in an asymptomatic adult. Ask about osmotic symptoms and weight loss, which would change urgency.

NICE NG28: for most adults, offer modified-release metformin with an SGLT2 inhibitor from diagnosis, introduced stepwise — metformin first to check tolerability, then the SGLT2 inhibitor. Doses per BNF. Set an individualised HbA1c target and review at 3–6 months.

Calculate QRISK3; NICE NG238 recommends atorvastatin 20 mg for primary prevention if QRISK3 is 10% or more. Confirm the BP with home or ambulatory readings (NICE NG136). Stopping smoking is the single largest risk reduction: behavioural support plus varenicline, cytisinicline or NRT, or a nicotine vape (NICE NG209).

The NHS Type 2 Diabetes Path to Remission Programme (England) offers total diet replacement to adults aged 18–65 diagnosed within the last 6 years with BMI 27 or more (25 or more for people from Black, Asian or other ethnic minority backgrounds). Remission is a realistic goal to offer, not a promise.

Car and van licence (Group 1): no need to tell the DVLA if treated by diet or tablets that do not cause hypoglycaemia, such as metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors. Lorry or bus licence (Group 2): the driver must tell the DVLA if treated with tablets that carry a hypoglycaemia risk (sulfonylureas or glinides). Insulin must be notified for both groups (Group 1 only if longer than 3 months). Ask what he drives.

Structured education at diagnosis (NICE NG28); foot risk assessment at diagnosis and at least annually (NICE NG19); referral to the NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme; U&E, ACR, lipids and BP at annual review.

Report marked thirst, passing large volumes of urine, weight loss, vomiting or drowsiness. SGLT2 inhibitors: stop when acutely unwell or dehydrated (sick-day rules) and seek help for vomiting, abdominal pain or breathlessness.

dg.d: Opened with his thoughts before the result; confirmed the diagnosis without either minimising or dwelling on complications.
Eleven-hour days in the van, garage food, energy drinks, smoking, self-employed with no sick pay, caring for his father at the end.
Confirmed two diagnostic HbA1c values; QRISK3 and lipids; HBPM or ABPM to confirm BP; U&E, ACR; eye screening and foot check.
Type 2 diabetes vs other types (slow onset, BMI 32, asymptomatic); asked what he drives to place him in the right DVLA group.
Asked about osmotic symptoms, weight loss and visual change; no features of hyperglycaemic emergency.
Stated: type 2 diabetes, early and asymptomatic, with modifiable cardiovascular risk from smoking, BP and cholesterol.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Dual first-line MR metformin + SGLT2 inhibitor, introduced stepwise (NICE NG28, February 2026); remission programme; structured education; one negotiated lifestyle goal.
Smoking cessation referral (NICE NG209); statin if QRISK3 10% or more (NICE NG238); BP confirmation (NICE NG136).
Named osmotic and SGLT2 inhibitor sick-day warning symptoms; 2-week review with BP readings; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “made my peace with where this goes” and “give me the tablets”, and the unspoken licence worry.
Idea (father’s path is fixed), concerns (early death, losing his licence and income), expectation (tablets and no fuss).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — fatalism/despair built on watching his father die of complications; plus an unspoken terror that the diagnosis will cost him his driving licence and his livelihood — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Errol, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for making time between drops. You’ve already guessed why we asked you in — before I say anything, tell me what’s going through your mind.
model.why: Opens with his perspective, not the result

model.text: It’s diabetes, isn’t it. My dad had it. Eyes, then his leg, then his heart at sixty-one. So I’ve made my peace with where this goes. Just give me the tablets and I’ll get on with it.

Yes, the two blood tests do confirm type 2 diabetes. I’m sorry about your dad — that’s a lot to have watched. I don’t want to just hand you a prescription today. Can we spend a few minutes on you, what this means, and a plan that fits your life?
model.why: Confirms the diagnosis honestly and sets an agenda beyond tablets

model.text: Go on. I’ve got till half past.
Tell me more about what happened with your dad.
Diagnosed in his forties. Never did anything about it — kept smoking, never went to the clinic. Blind in one eye, lost his leg below the knee at 58, heart attack at 61. I looked after him at the end.
Thank you. That tells me a lot. Have you had any symptoms yourself — very thirsty, up at night to pass water, losing weight without trying, blurred vision, sores that won’t heal?
model.why: Screens for symptomatic hyperglycaemia and complications

model.text: Tired, that’s why I came. Nothing else really.
Talk me through a normal working day — food, drink, how much you’re sitting.
In the van eleven hours. Garage food — pasties, meal deals. Energy drinks to keep going. Ten fags a day. No time for exercise with this job.
That sounds like the job is running you, rather than you being lazy. What do you drive — a van, or anything over three and a half tonnes?
model.why: Establishes licence group for the DVLA advice

model.text: Just a Transit. Why?
I’ll come to that. Can I ask — has anything about this diagnosis worried you that you haven’t said yet?
(Pause.) My mate said they take your licence off you if you go on insulin. I’m self-employed. No van, no money.
I’m really glad you said that. So there are two worries: that you’re on your dad’s path whatever you do, and that this could cost you your living. What were you hoping for today?
model.why: Summarises both hidden concerns and checks expectations

model.text: Honestly? Tablets and not much fuss. There’s no point pretending I’m going to be a gym bloke.

Let me answer the licence first. On a van licence, with diet or the tablets I’d suggest, you don’t even need to tell the DVLA. You keep driving and you keep earning. Insulin has extra rules, but they’re manageable, and we’re nowhere near that.
model.why: Accurate, proactive DVLA advice for Group 1

model.text: Right. That’s a weight off, honestly.

Now your dad. What happened to him came from years of high sugar, high blood pressure and smoking left untreated, in a different era. You’ve been caught early, with no symptoms, kidneys and eyes working. The eyes, feet and heart can largely be protected if we control those things. That’s a very different starting line.
model.why: Reframes fatalism with accurate information on modifiable risk

model.text: He never went to a single check-up.
And you’re here. The biggest thing for your heart isn’t the sugar — it’s the cigarettes. Would you be open to help with stopping, not today necessarily, but properly?
model.why: Prioritises smoking cessation as the highest-yield action

model.text: I’ve thought about it. Since Dad. Maybe.

Then here’s what I suggest, and tell me what fits. A tablet called metformin, the slow-release kind, starting now; once it’s settled, a second tablet that also protects the heart and kidneys. A cholesterol check with your heart-risk score, and a home blood pressure monitor for a week, because today’s reading is borderline.
model.why: Dual first-line therapy introduced stepwise: MR metformin, then the SGLT2 inhibitor once metformin is tolerated (NICE NG28 2026); QRISK3 and BP confirmation

model.text: Two tablets? I thought it was just the one.

The newer guidance starts both early because they protect more than the sugar. And there’s something your dad was never offered: with your weight and an early diagnosis, type 2 can sometimes go into remission — sugar back to normal off medication. There’s an NHS programme for that. Would you want me to refer you?
model.why: Offers remission via the NHS Path to Remission Programme

model.text: Remission? I didn’t know that was a thing. Yeah, go on.
Good. And one small change you choose for this week — not a list from me. What could you realistically do on the road?
Swap the energy drinks for water. I could do that.

Perfect. I’ll also book a diabetes education course, eye screening and a foot check — they catch problems years before they matter. The stop-smoking team will ring you if you’re happy for me to refer.
Fine. Refer me.

If you get very thirsty, are passing lots of urine, lose weight, or once you’re on the second tablet feel very unwell with vomiting or tummy pain, stop that tablet and ring us the same day, or 111 out of hours. I’ll see you in two weeks with the blood pressure readings.
model.why: Specific safety-net including SGLT2 inhibitor sick-day advice

model.text: Two weeks. Okay.
When you get home and someone asks what the doctor said, what will you tell them?
It’s diabetes but it’s early. I keep my licence. Tablets, water not energy drinks, a course, and they’ll help me pack in the fags. And I’m not my dad.

social.t: Self-employed, no sick pay, eleven hours a day in the van. Plans must fit the road: garage food swaps, short walks at drops, appointments he can make.
He nursed his father through complications and death. Bereavement and anticipatory fear shape how he hears every sentence about diabetes.

legal.t: Group 1 (car or van up to 3.5 tonnes): no notification if treated by diet or tablets not carrying hypoglycaemia risk. Group 2 (lorry or bus): must notify if treated with tablets carrying hypoglycaemia risk (sulfonylureas or glinides). Insulin: must notify (Group 1 only if treatment will last over 3 months). Sulfonylureas bring glucose monitoring requirements.
In England, diabetes treated with medication qualifies for a medical exemption certificate, so his tablets would be free once he applies.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024) and NICE NG197: explain the options, including remission and the reasons for dual therapy, and agree the plan with him rather than for him.
NICE NG209: advise stopping at every opportunity and offer referral to stop-smoking services with behavioural support and medicines or a nicotine vape. Record his decision.

community.t: NHS Type 2 Diabetes Path to Remission Programme; local structured education (for example DESMOND); NHS Stop Smoking services and community pharmacy; Diabetes UK for plain-language information.

redFlags: Marked thirst, polyuria, rapid weight loss, vomiting or drowsiness — possible hyperglycaemic emergency, same-day assessment
Slim build, rapid onset or ketosis — question whether this is type 2
Visual loss, foot ulcer or chest pain — complications needing urgent assessment
psychosocial: Fatalism from watching his father’s decline and death
Self-employed driver: fear of losing his licence and income
Diet, energy drinks and inactivity shaped by long days in the van; smoking
ice: Idea: “Diabetes took my dad’s eyes, leg and heart — it’ll do the same to me.”
Concern: early death, and that the diagnosis will cost him his licence and living
Expectation: tablets with no fuss — underneath, to hear that his father’s ending isn’t fixed

playbook.diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 71 then 69 mmol/mol), asymptomatic, with obesity (BMI 32), current smoking, borderline BP needing confirmation and a cholesterol needing QRISK3 assessment. No evidence of renal disease on current tests.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your blood sugar has been running too high for a while — that’s type 2 diabetes. It’s early, you have no damage we know of, and the things that hurt your dad — sugar, blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking — are all things we can change.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve told me you’ve made your peace with your dad’s ending. I don’t think it’s yours. And your licence is safe with these tablets.”
management.psychosocial: Build every step around the van: one chosen swap (water for energy drinks), walking at drops, appointments he can make; smoking support when he’s ready.
sharedPlan: Dual first-line (NICE NG28, February 2026): MR metformin now, SGLT2 inhibitor added once metformin is tolerated; structured education
QRISK3 and statin discussion (NICE NG238); home BP readings (NICE NG136); smoking cessation referral (NICE NG209)
Path to Remission Programme referral; eye screening and foot check booked (NICE NG19)
safetyNet: Thirst, polyuria, weight loss, vomiting, abdominal pain or drowsiness — same-day contact, 111 out of hours
Stop the SGLT2 inhibitor if acutely unwell or dehydrated; review in 2 weeks with BP readings

pitfalls.intro: Almost every candidate can prescribe metformin. This station is passed or failed on whether you hear the fatalism and the licence fear under “just give me the tablets”.

items.fail: Taking “just give me the tablets” at face value and prescribing.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” His father’s death is the engine of the consultation; a prescription into despair changes nothing.
items.fix: Ask about his father first: “Tell me what happened to him.” Then reframe with facts.

items.fail: Giving no DVLA advice, or telling him he must inform the DVLA.
items.why: Wrong advice for a Group 1 driver on non-hypoglycaemic tablets, and it leaves his main hidden fear unaddressed.
items.fix: Ask what he drives, then say clearly: van licence, these tablets, no notification needed.

items.fail: Focusing only on HbA1c and ignoring smoking, BP and cholesterol.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Cardiovascular disease is the main threat; NICE NG238, NG136 and NG209 all apply.
items.fix: Name smoking as the biggest single step, calculate QRISK3, and confirm the BP with home readings.

items.fail: Metformin alone with no mention of the updated NICE NG28 approach.
items.why: NICE NG28 recommends MR metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor for most adults, introduced stepwise.
items.fix: Explain the two-step plan simply and why the second tablet protects the heart and kidneys.

items.fail: A generic lifestyle lecture: salmon, gyms and 150 minutes a week.
items.why: “Advice not tailored to the patient’s circumstances.” He sits in a van eleven hours a day.
items.fix: Ask him to choose one change that works on the road, and build from there at review.

items.fail: No safety-net and no booked review.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement; new SGLT2 inhibitor users need sick-day advice.
items.fix: Name osmotic symptoms and the SGLT2 inhibitor sick-day rule, and book review in two weeks.

That sounds like the job is running you, rather than you being lazy. What do you drive — a van, or anything over three and a half tonnes?
SCA_MODELS.why: Establishes licence group for the DVLA advice

SCA_MODELS.text: Just a Transit. Why?
I’ll come to that. Can I ask — has anything about this diagnosis worried you that you haven’t said yet?
(Pause.) My mate said they take your licence off you if you go on insulin. I’m self-employed. No van, no money.
I’m really glad you said that. So there are two worries: that you’re on your dad’s path whatever you do, and that this could cost you your living. What were you hoping for today?
SCA_MODELS.why: Summarises both hidden concerns and checks expectations

SCA_MODELS.text: Honestly? Tablets and not much fuss. There’s no point pretending I’m going to be a gym bloke.

Let me answer the licence first. On a van licence, with diet or the tablets I’d suggest, you don’t even need to tell the DVLA. You keep driving and you keep earning. Insulin has extra rules, but they’re manageable, and we’re nowhere near that.
SCA_MODELS.why: Accurate, proactive DVLA advice for Group 1

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. That’s a weight off, honestly.

Now your dad. What happened to him came from years of high sugar, high blood pressure and smoking left untreated, in a different era. You’ve been caught early, with no symptoms, kidneys and eyes working. The eyes, feet and heart can largely be protected if we control those things. That’s a very different starting line.
SCA_MODELS.why: Reframes fatalism with accurate information on modifiable risk

SCA_MODELS.text: He never went to a single check-up.
And you’re here. The biggest thing for your heart isn’t the sugar — it’s the cigarettes. Would you be open to help with stopping, not today necessarily, but properly?
SCA_MODELS.why: Prioritises smoking cessation as the highest-yield action

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ve thought about it. Since Dad. Maybe.

Then here’s what I suggest, and tell me what fits. A tablet called metformin, the slow-release kind, starting now; once it’s settled, a second tablet that also protects the heart and kidneys. A cholesterol check with your heart-risk score, and a home blood pressure monitor for a week, because today’s reading is borderline.
SCA_MODELS.why: Dual first-line therapy introduced stepwise: MR metformin, then the SGLT2 inhibitor once metformin is tolerated (NICE NG28 2026); QRISK3 and BP confirmation

SCA_MODELS.text: Two tablets? I thought it was just the one.

The newer guidance starts both early because they protect more than the sugar. And there’s something your dad was never offered: with your weight and an early diagnosis, type 2 can sometimes go into remission — sugar back to normal off medication. There’s an NHS programme for that. Would you want me to refer you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Offers remission via the NHS Path to Remission Programme

SCA_MODELS.text: Remission? I didn’t know that was a thing. Yeah, go on.
Good. And one small change you choose for this week — not a list from me. What could you realistically do on the road?
Swap the energy drinks for water. I could do that.

Perfect. I’ll also book a diabetes education course, eye screening and a foot check — they catch problems years before they matter. The stop-smoking team will ring you if you’re happy for me to refer.
Fine. Refer me.

If you get very thirsty, are passing lots of urine, lose weight, or once you’re on the second tablet feel very unwell with vomiting or tummy pain, stop that tablet and ring us the same day, or 111 out of hours. I’ll see you in two weeks with the blood pressure readings.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net including SGLT2 inhibitor sick-day advice

SCA_MODELS.text: Two weeks. Okay.
When you get home and someone asks what the doctor said, what will you tell them?
It’s diabetes but it’s early. I keep my licence. Tablets, water not energy drinks, a course, and they’ll help me pack in the fags. And I’m not my dad.

SCA_STEM.name: Errol Bennett
SCA_STEM.recent: Bloods for tiredness: HbA1c 71 mmol/mol; repeat HbA1c 69 mmol/mol. Total cholesterol 5.9 mmol/L. eGFR and urine ACR normal. BMI 32. Clinic BP 142/88 mmHg. Self-employed delivery driver.
SCA_STEM.reason: Booked by reception to discuss results.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG28 (updated February 2026) · NICE NG19 · NICE NG238 · NICE NG136 · NICE NG209 · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (diabetes)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Two HbA1c results of 48 mmol/mol or more confirm type 2 diabetes. The first consultation sets engagement for years: treat the fatalism, answer the licence fear, then build a plan around his working day.

points.t: HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol or more on two occasions confirms diabetes in an asymptomatic adult. Ask about osmotic symptoms and weight loss, which would change urgency.

NICE NG28: for most adults, offer modified-release metformin with an SGLT2 inhibitor from diagnosis, introduced stepwise — metformin first to check tolerability, then the SGLT2 inhibitor. Doses per BNF. Set an individualised HbA1c target and review at 3–6 months.

Calculate QRISK3; NICE NG238 recommends atorvastatin 20 mg for primary prevention if QRISK3 is 10% or more. Confirm the BP with home or ambulatory readings (NICE NG136). Stopping smoking is the single largest risk reduction: behavioural support plus varenicline, cytisinicline or NRT, or a nicotine vape (NICE NG209).

The NHS Type 2 Diabetes Path to Remission Programme (England) offers total diet replacement to adults aged 18–65 diagnosed within the last 6 years with BMI 27 or more (25 or more for people from Black, Asian or other ethnic minority backgrounds). Remission is a realistic goal to offer, not a promise.

Car and van licence (Group 1): no need to tell the DVLA if treated by diet or tablets that do not cause hypoglycaemia, such as metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors. Lorry or bus licence (Group 2): the driver must tell the DVLA if treated with tablets that carry a hypoglycaemia risk (sulfonylureas or glinides). Insulin must be notified for both groups (Group 1 only if longer than 3 months). Ask what he drives.

Structured education at diagnosis (NICE NG28); foot risk assessment at diagnosis and at least annually (NICE NG19); referral to the NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme; U&E, ACR, lipids and BP at annual review.

Report marked thirst, passing large volumes of urine, weight loss, vomiting or drowsiness. SGLT2 inhibitors: stop when acutely unwell or dehydrated (sick-day rules) and seek help for vomiting, abdominal pain or breathlessness.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Opened with his thoughts before the result; confirmed the diagnosis without either minimising or dwelling on complications.
Eleven-hour days in the van, garage food, energy drinks, smoking, self-employed with no sick pay, caring for his father at the end.
Picked up “made my peace with where this goes” and “give me the tablets”, and the unspoken licence worry.
Idea (father’s path is fixed), concerns (early death, losing his licence and income), expectation (tablets and no fuss).
Confirmed two diagnostic HbA1c values; QRISK3 and lipids; HBPM or ABPM to confirm BP; U&E, ACR; eye screening and foot check.
Type 2 diabetes vs other types (slow onset, BMI 32, asymptomatic); asked what he drives to place him in the right DVLA group.
Asked about osmotic symptoms, weight loss and visual change; no features of hyperglycaemic emergency.
Stated: type 2 diabetes, early and asymptomatic, with modifiable cardiovascular risk from smoking, BP and cholesterol.
Dual first-line MR metformin + SGLT2 inhibitor, introduced stepwise (NICE NG28, February 2026); remission programme; structured education; one negotiated lifestyle goal.
Smoking cessation referral (NICE NG209); statin if QRISK3 10% or more (NICE NG238); BP confirmation (NICE NG136).
Named osmotic and SGLT2 inhibitor sick-day warning symptoms; 2-week review with BP readings; teach-back.

social.t: Self-employed, no sick pay, eleven hours a day in the van. Plans must fit the road: garage food swaps, short walks at drops, appointments he can make.
He nursed his father through complications and death. Bereavement and anticipatory fear shape how he hears every sentence about diabetes.

legal.t: Group 1 (car or van up to 3.5 tonnes): no notification if treated by diet or tablets not carrying hypoglycaemia risk. Group 2 (lorry or bus): must notify if treated with tablets carrying hypoglycaemia risk (sulfonylureas or glinides). Insulin: must notify (Group 1 only if treatment will last over 3 months). Sulfonylureas bring glucose monitoring requirements.
In England, diabetes treated with medication qualifies for a medical exemption certificate, so his tablets would be free once he applies.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024) and NICE NG197: explain the options, including remission and the reasons for dual therapy, and agree the plan with him rather than for him.
NICE NG209: advise stopping at every opportunity and offer referral to stop-smoking services with behavioural support and medicines or a nicotine vape. Record his decision.

community.t: NHS Type 2 Diabetes Path to Remission Programme; local structured education (for example DESMOND); NHS Stop Smoking services and community pharmacy; Diabetes UK for plain-language information.

redFlags: Marked thirst, polyuria, rapid weight loss, vomiting or drowsiness — possible hyperglycaemic emergency, same-day assessment
Slim build, rapid onset or ketosis — question whether this is type 2
Visual loss, foot ulcer or chest pain — complications needing urgent assessment
psychosocial: Fatalism from watching his father’s decline and death
Self-employed driver: fear of losing his licence and income
Diet, energy drinks and inactivity shaped by long days in the van; smoking
ice: Idea: “Diabetes took my dad’s eyes, leg and heart — it’ll do the same to me.”
Concern: early death, and that the diagnosis will cost him his licence and living
Expectation: tablets with no fuss — underneath, to hear that his father’s ending isn’t fixed

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 71 then 69 mmol/mol), asymptomatic, with obesity (BMI 32), current smoking, borderline BP needing confirmation and a cholesterol needing QRISK3 assessment. No evidence of renal disease on current tests.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your blood sugar has been running too high for a while — that’s type 2 diabetes. It’s early, you have no damage we know of, and the things that hurt your dad — sugar, blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking — are all things we can change.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve told me you’ve made your peace with your dad’s ending. I don’t think it’s yours. And your licence is safe with these tablets.”
management.psychosocial: Build every step around the van: one chosen swap (water for energy drinks), walking at drops, appointments he can make; smoking support when he’s ready.
sharedPlan: Dual first-line (NICE NG28, February 2026): MR metformin now, SGLT2 inhibitor added once metformin is tolerated; structured education
QRISK3 and statin discussion (NICE NG238); home BP readings (NICE NG136); smoking cessation referral (NICE NG209)
Path to Remission Programme referral; eye screening and foot check booked (NICE NG19)
safetyNet: Thirst, polyuria, weight loss, vomiting, abdominal pain or drowsiness — same-day contact, 111 out of hours
Stop the SGLT2 inhibitor if acutely unwell or dehydrated; review in 2 weeks with BP readings

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Almost every candidate can prescribe metformin. This station is passed or failed on whether you hear the fatalism and the licence fear under “just give me the tablets”.

items.fail: Taking “just give me the tablets” at face value and prescribing.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” His father’s death is the engine of the consultation; a prescription into despair changes nothing.
items.fix: Ask about his father first: “Tell me what happened to him.” Then reframe with facts.

items.fail: Giving no DVLA advice, or telling him he must inform the DVLA.
items.why: Wrong advice for a Group 1 driver on non-hypoglycaemic tablets, and it leaves his main hidden fear unaddressed.
items.fix: Ask what he drives, then say clearly: van licence, these tablets, no notification needed.

items.fail: Focusing only on HbA1c and ignoring smoking, BP and cholesterol.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Cardiovascular disease is the main threat; NICE NG238, NG136 and NG209 all apply.
items.fix: Name smoking as the biggest single step, calculate QRISK3, and confirm the BP with home readings.

items.fail: Metformin alone with no mention of the updated NICE NG28 approach.
items.why: NICE NG28 recommends MR metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor for most adults, introduced stepwise.
items.fix: Explain the two-step plan simply and why the second tablet protects the heart and kidneys.

items.fail: A generic lifestyle lecture: salmon, gyms and 150 minutes a week.
items.why: “Advice not tailored to the patient’s circumstances.” He sits in a van eleven hours a day.
items.fix: Ask him to choose one change that works on the road, and build from there at review.

items.fail: No safety-net and no booked review.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement; new SGLT2 inhibitor users need sick-day advice.
items.fix: Name osmotic symptoms and the SGLT2 inhibitor sick-day rule, and book review in two weeks.
